div.div:
Workflow:You create a Fargate Profile in AWS that says:
"Any pod in the staging namespace with the label type: serverless should run on Fargate."
You submit a standard Pod YAML to the API Server.The EKS Mutating Webhook sees your pod, matches it against your profile,
and automatically injects schedulerName: fargate-scheduler into your Pod spec before it ever reaches the scheduling phase.

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe center; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding-top: 595px; margin-left: 2px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 17px; font-family: Helvetica; color: light-dark(#000000, #ffffff); line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; font-weight: bold; white-space: nowrap;

div.div:
How Pods reach the right scheduler
The API Server does not route Pods; it just stores them. Every scheduler watches for unscheduled Pods (no nodeName yet) and only picks up the ones whose schedulerName matches its own name, like separate "buckets".
Bucket A (default-scheduler): The standard kube-scheduler (running on the control plane) takes these and places them on EC2 nodes.
Bucket B (fargate-scheduler): The AWS Fargate scheduler takes only these, ignores Bucket A, and spins up a dedicated micro-VM for each one.
